text: Friedrich Wilhelm Ernst Paulus (23 September 1890 – 1 February 1957) was a German Generalfeldmarschall during World War II, best known for the surrender of the German 6th Army during the Battle of Stalingrad (July 1942 to February 1943). The battle ended in disaster for the Wehrmacht, with Soviet forces encircling the Germans within Stalingrad, resulting in the death or capture of most of the 265,000-strong 6th Army, their Axis allies, and collaborators. Paulus had fought in World War I in France and the Balkans, rising to captain by the war's end. After the armistice, he served in the Reichswehr as a brigade adjutant and was selected among 4,000 officers allowed to serve in the limited defensive army. He joined the 13th Infantry Regiment at Stuttgart and held various staff positions from 1921 to 1933, including guest lectures in Moscow during the 1920s as part of military cooperation between the Weimar Republic and the Soviet Union. In 1934–35, he briefly commanded a motorized battalion; in October 1935, he became chief of staff at Panzer Troop Command, overseeing the training of the Panzerwaffe. In February 1938, he was appointed chief of staff to General Heinz Guderian’s XVI Army Corps, where Guderian praised his intelligence and diligence but expressed doubts about his decisiveness and command experience. Paulus remained in that role until May 1939, when he was promoted to major general and became chief of staff for the German Tenth Army, which later became the Sixth Army. He saw action in the invasions of Poland and the Low Countries and was promoted to lieutenant general in August 1940. In November 1941, after Field Marshal Walter von Reichenau, his patron, was reassigned, Paulus was promoted to General der Panzertruppe and appointed commander of the Sixth Army, taking command on 20 January 1942, six days after Reichenau’s death. Paulus led the drive on Stalingrad, where his troops engaged in over three months of brutal urban warfare. In November 1942, during Operation Uranus, the Soviet Red Army launched a massive counter-offensive that surrounded the 6th Army. Paulus refused to request evacuation and followed Hitler’s orders to hold Stalingrad at all costs. Operation Winter Storm, a relief effort by Army Group Don under Field Marshal Erich von Manstein, was launched in December, but Paulus was not given permission to break out, and Manstein’s forces failed to reach Stalingrad due to Soviet offensives elsewhere. Kurt Zeitzler eventually convinced Hitler to allow a breakout, provided Paulus continued to hold Stalingrad—an impossible task. For two months, Paulus and his forces fought on, but the lack of food, ammunition, and deteriorating conditions gradually weakened the defense. On 7 January 1943, General Konstantin Rokossovsky offered surrender terms, including normal rations, medical care, and retention of badges and uniforms. Paulus requested permission from Hitler to surrender, but the High Command rejected the request, stating that holding out helped the entire front. On 25 January, after the Soviets overran the last airstrip, Paulus again requested permission, emphasizing that his men were without food or ammunition, with 18,000 wounded, and that collapse was inevitable. Hitler rejected the request once more and ordered Paulus to hold Stalingrad to the death. On 30 January, Paulus informed Hitler that his forces were only hours from collapse. Hitler responded by promoting Paulus to field marshal, noting there was no precedent of a German field marshal being captured alive, implying Paulus must commit suicide. On 31 January 1943, Paulus and his staff surrendered. According to Colonel Wilhelm Adam’s diary, Paulus read the promotion order and said, “One can't help feeling it's an invitation to suicide. However I'm not going to do them such a favour,” before learning that Soviet forces were at the door. He recorded his new rank in official documents, stamped them with the seal, and threw the seal into a fire. The Soviet general informed Paulus that they would take him to the rear at 9:00, and he was transported in his personal car. The surrender marked the end of the 6th Army’s resistance. On 2 February 1943, the remainder of the army formally capitulated. Hitler was enraged by the surrender, vowing never to appoint another field marshal, though he later appointed seven more during the war’s final years. Hitler claimed that 18,000 to 20,000 Germans committed suicide annually in peacetime, and questioned how Paulus could surrender when 50,000 to 60,000 soldiers had died defending Stalingrad. Paulus, a Roman Catholic, opposed suicide and told General Max Pfeffer, “I have no intention of shooting myself for this Bohemian corporal,” and forbade his soldiers from standing on their trenches to be shot. Before surrendering, he sent his wedding ring back to his wife, who died in 1949 while he remained in captivity. Initially refusing to collaborate with the Soviets, Paulus became a vocal critic of the Nazi regime after the July 1944 assassination attempt, joining the Soviet-sponsored National Committee for a Free Germany. As a result, his wife and daughter Olga von Kutzschenbach were placed under Sippenhaft. He later served as a witness for the prosecution at the Nuremberg Trials. In 1953, he moved to East Germany, where he worked in military history research and lived in Dresden. At the Nuremberg Trials, when asked about the Stalingrad prisoners, he told a journalist to inform the wives and mothers that their husbands and sons were well. However, of the 100,000 German prisoners taken at Stalingrad, half died during the march to Siberian camps, nearly as many died in captivity, and only about 6,000 survived and returned home. In a 1954 talk in Berlin titled "On the vital issues of our nation," Paulus honored General Heinz Guderian, whom he had served with as chief of staff for the armored forces, and criticized the political leadership of the German Empire and Nazi Germany for causing military defeats in both world wars. He noted that Germany had great military experts like Clausewitz, Moltke the Elder, and Schlieffen, who assessed the political-military situation with sobriety, but that even the best army fails when ordered to perform impossible tasks. He also criticized U.S. foreign policy as aggressive and called for reconciliation between Germany and France, stating that German-French relations must be resolved to prevent the U.S. from using the conflict between the two nations as a tool of dominance.

American policy is described as "power politics," a concept that deeply affects Germans, who have experienced the consequences of pursuing aggressive, forceful strategies that prioritize national strength at the expense of others. Germans have learned from the 20th century that such policies inevitably fail unless they suppress the national will and independence of other peoples. The idea that the age of nations has ended because the United States relies on such dominance is a misconception and dangerous. Establishing positive neighborly relations with neighboring countries, especially France, is essential for Germany's national survival. The old enmity and disputes between Germany and France must be permanently resolved, as their relationship is a key link in the American strategy of dividing European nations and using them as tools for U.S. policy. Former Chancellor Heinrich Brüning advocated for improved relations between West Germany and the Eastern Bloc, criticizing West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer's pro-American stance and opposing the EDC and Bonn conventions. Brüning supported negotiating with the East whenever possible, and another prominent German politician agreed that final implementation of the EDC agreement would be harmful to the German nation, arguing that no reasonable person can understand why Adenauer, under American influence, resists opportunities for economic and cultural engagement with Eastern peoples. As a former military officer and sector commander, based on his experiences, Paulus concluded that Germany must pursue any path leading to strengthened East-West relations. He emphasized that focusing on German unity, independence, and the affirmation of national rights best serves peace, international détente, and reconciliation. Good relations with other nations that respect Germany's rights are essential for European collective security and a prosperous future for Germany. A reunited Germany with balanced relations with the two major powers would ensure European peace and lay the foundation for general prosperity. From 1953 to 1956, Paulus lived in Dresden, East Germany, where he served as the civilian chief of the East German Military History Research Institute. In late 1956, he was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and gradually became weaker. He died in Dresden on 1 February 1957, at the age of 66. According to his last will, his body was transported to Baden-Baden, West Germany, to be buried at the Hauptfriedhof next to his wife.
